F37.quote: The project director, Scott Rettberg, reflects on the process involved in developing the database and the challenges involved in continuing to document the ever-changing landscape of the field of electronic literature.
F37.claim: Scott Rettberg, the project director, the essay's author

F38.quote: The ELMCIP project (Electronic Literature as a Model of Creativity and Innovation in Practice: Developing a Network-Based Creativity Community), which ran from 2010-2013, was one of the most ambitious joint research projects to date in the field of electronic literature (e-lit).
F38.claim: the project ran 2010–2013, one of the field's most ambitious joint research projects

F39.quote: The seven-partner, six-nation project resulted in conferences in six countries, a major exhibition, three books, a film, the first digital anthology of European electronic literature, and the ELMCIP Electronic Literature Knowledge Base, a large-scale, open-access research database.
F39.claim: seven partners, six nations; conferences, an exhibition, three books, a film, an anthology and the knowledge base
F39.mark: contested (partner count: B2 F22 'seven European academic research partners and one non-academic partner')

F40.quote: The Knowledge Base is now a decade old. It has developed for seven years beyond the funded project period and has grown into an essential research infrastructure for the field.
F40.claim: a decade old in 2021, developed seven years beyond the funded period, an essential research infrastructure

F41.quote: Even so, like many DH projects, it exists in a state of precarity, within an institution that, like many others, has only begun to confront the challenges of hosting and preserving DH infrastructure for a long lifespan.
F41.claim: it exists in a state of precarity, its institution only beginning to confront long-term hosting

F42.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F42.quote: The Knowledge Base is intended to document electronic literature as a dynamic field of practice, one whose cultural import becomes more comprehensible when the activities of authors, scholars, publications, performances, and exhibitions can be related to each other, in multiple configurations.
F42.claim: its purpose: to document electronic literature as a dynamic field of practice whose activities can be related

F43.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F43.quote: When a record of a critical article is documented in the Knowledge Base, all the creative works it references are noted, and cross-references then automatically appear on the record for the work itself.
F43.claim: a critical article's referenced works are noted and cross-references appear automatically on each work's record

F44.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F44.quote: The Knowledge Base makes perceptible interactions between human and nonhuman actors, and documents the diverse range of artistic, scholarly, and pedagogical practices in the field of electronic literature.
F44.claim: it makes perceptible interactions between human and nonhuman actors

F45.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F45.quote: The majority of the information in the database can be accessed by anyone with an Internet connection, without logging in. … We create contributor accounts on request for any researcher or writer working in the field.
F45.claim: open access without login; contributor accounts on request for any researcher or writer

F46.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F46.quote: By documenting actants and activities they deem significant, we can present the Knowledge Base as a collectively authored, networked research environment.
F46.claim: a collectively authored, networked research environment

F47.locus: Developing a conceptual model of a field
F47.quote: we realized that we were developing a conceptual model of the field as a whole. … A distinctive aspect of the Knowledge Base is that it tracks relations between different types of objects and actors and makes those visible and pliable to researchers.
F47.claim: a conceptual model of the whole field, tracking relations between objects and actors

F48.quote: From the standpoint of researchers and teachers, memory is more important than novelty, as true novelty is not possible without understanding the past.
F48.claim: memory is more important than novelty for the field

F49.quote: the idea that both literary community and the literary artifact itself can be understood as networks of relations. … a poetry generator that is an algorithmic structure that assembles poetry from arrays of possible verse. … The literary ecology that results in the creative practices of electronic literature can be understood as a network of networks, encompassing human and machine intelligence, social practices and affiliations, software platforms, ad hoc alliances, and formalized institutions.
F49.claim: community and artifact as networks of relations; a poetry generator as an algorithmic structure; a network of networks encompassing human and machine intelligence

F50.quote: The scope of the database is thus such that it will always be incomplete.
F50.claim: its scope will always be incomplete

F51.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F51.quote: It is structurally similar to a Wiki in the sense that contributors must have an account to add or edit records, but once they do, they can edit and enhance any existing record.
F51.claim: wiki-like: any contributor with an account can edit any record

F52.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F52.quote: the ELMCIP Knowledge Base largely leaves subjective description, literary analysis, and interpretation to the critics. … Thus, in comparison to the ELD, the Knowledge Base is driven more by discovery than by edification.
F52.claim: it leaves description and interpretation to the critics; driven by discovery more than edification (against the ELD)

F53.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F53.quote: creative works, critical writing, authors, platform/software, teaching resources, publishers and journals, organizations, events, databases and archives, and research collections.

F54.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F54.quote: This results in a great deal of incomplete information in the database … they would likely only create a “stub” record with the most basic information.
F54.claim: autocomplete fields produce stub records and incomplete information

F55.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F55.quote: Records come into the database in a variety of different ways: primarily through the contributions of researchers in the field, but also in a more concentrated way through the course “Digital Humanities in Practice” at the University of Bergen.
F55.claim: records come from researchers' contributions and a University of Bergen course

F56.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F56.quote: its coverage will always be partial and will always be biased by the scope of the research of individual researchers.
F56.claim: its coverage will always be partial and biased by individual researchers' scope

F57.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F57.quote: Ikeda notes that when he searches the ELMCIP database for terms like “blackness,” “race,” and “racialization” he comes up with zero search results (Ikeda 2020). … Ikeda argues that this absence is one piece of evidence of “white supremacy” in the institutions of e-lit.
F57.claim: Ikeda's report of zero results for 'blackness', 'race', 'racialization', read as evidence of white supremacy in e-lit's institutions
F57.mark: contested (B3 F58: the author finds five results for 'race')

F58.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F58.quote: Actually, a search for “race” does in fact turn up some results, but only five, and “Blackness for Sale” was not there. … While I think Ikeda perhaps goes a step too far in labelling the field of electronic literature thus, the broader lacuna is one worth considering in the context of the database
F58.claim: five results for 'race' and Blackness for Sale absent; the lacuna worth considering

F59.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F59.quote: The Knowledge Base has “controlled vocabularies” for core bibliographic information, but not for themes and content descriptions. … each individual contributor tags the records they contribute or develop using an uncontrolled vocabulary.
F59.claim: controlled vocabularies for bibliographic data; uncontrolled folksonomic tags for themes

F60.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F60.quote: a database is a model of the field that it represents, which recursively impacts that field in the process of modeling it.
F60.claim: a database is a model of its field that recursively impacts the field

F61.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F61.quote: for the most part, authors’ names and brief biographical information are gathered from other publicly available sources. … But our general policy now is that we will not indicate an author’s gender unless they specifically declare that information themselves while editing the record.
F61.claim: authors' names gathered from public sources; gender shown only where the author declares it

F62.locus: The risks and affordances of an open knowledge community
F62.quote: currently all the records in the database are entered by humans rather than harvested by an automatic survey of references (Seiça 2016). … Nevertheless, the Knowledge Base is the most extensive record of citations available to the field. It will never be complete
F62.claim: all records entered by humans, none harvested automatically; the field's most extensive record of citations, never complete

F63.locus: Database development as constructive experimental research
F63.quote: A research collection can gather together any type of record in the database along with descriptive or analytical text.
F63.claim: a research collection gathers any records with descriptive or analytical text

F64.locus: Database development as constructive experimental research
F64.quote: “Can we identify an emerging canon of electronic literature based on all of the citations of creative works from critical writing documented in the database?” … This type of distant reading activity would not be possible for electronic literature without the large body of documentation and relational data the Knowledge Base contains.
F64.claim: data-mining and distant reading of citation patterns, e.g. an emerging canon

F65.locus: Long-term sustainability, data sharing, and the afterlife
F65.quote: considerable time and energy that would be better spent developing the content of the database has had to go into a seemingly endless quest for support to maintain a basic level of funding for maintenance and development of the platform itself.
F65.claim: an endless quest for basic funding of maintenance

F66.locus: Long-term sustainability, data sharing, and the afterlife
F66.quote: When planning any DH project or research infrastructure, it is wise to plan for a regenerative end state. … Whatever platform a database is developed in will eventually become obsolete.
F66.claim: plan for a regenerative end state; every platform becomes obsolete

F67.locus: Long-term sustainability, data sharing, and the afterlife
F67.quote: The CELL consortium includes 11 different organizations, research labs, and research centers … all of the CELL members have agreed that should one of the databases or archives lose its funding or otherwise reach its end of life, we will commit to migrating its data to another platform within the consortium.
F67.claim: CELL's 11 members commit to migrate a member database's data at its end of life

F68.quote: The database is not only there to be searched, and it is not only there to be read: it is there to be written, by all of us.
F68.claim: the database is there to be written by all

F69.locus: Long-term sustainability, data sharing, and the afterlife
F69.quote: At the University of Bergen, we are going through a slow process of developing a support structure in which the University Library takes on the long-term mission of supporting and maintaining DH research projects and infrastructures that are first developed by researchers and research projects.
F69.claim: the University Library slowly taking on long-term support

F70.locus: Background on ELMCIP Collaborative Research Project
F70.quote: ELMCIP also contributed to the development of an international Consortium of Electronic Literature (CELL) developing databases and archives of electronic literature around the world.
F70.claim: the project contributed to the development of CELL

F71.locus: Background on ELMCIP Collaborative Research Project
F71.quote: By the end of the ELMCIP project the Knowledge Base had become the most extensive online research resource in the international field.
F71.claim: by 2013 the most extensive online research resource in the field

F72.locus: Background on ELMCIP Collaborative Research Project
F72.quote: The Knowledge Base has grown from a narrower focus on representing European electronic literature and critical discourse – which grew almost immediately to encompass American electronic literature in its scope – to a broader international focus.
F72.claim: from European to American to international scope

F73.claim: a review of the knowledge base, which states its funding by the HERA programme
